label: thm:dense
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:dense}
Let $1<s\le2$ and let $E\subset C[0,1]$ be finite-dimensional, with $E\setminus\{0\}\subsetH_s[0,1]$. Then there is a dense vector subspace $M\subset C[0,1]$ such that
\[E\subset M,\qquad \dim M=\mathfrak c,\qquad M\setminus\{0\}\subsetH_s[0,1].\]
Consequently, $H_s[0,1]$ is $(n,\mathfrak c)$-dense-lineable for every $n\in\mathbb N$ and maximal pointwise dense-lineable in $C[0,1]$.
head: environment

label: lem:c0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:c0}
Let $K\subset[0,1]$ be compact and let $d=\dim_{\rm H} K>0$. There is a linear isometry $\Phi:c_0\to C(K)$ such that
\[\dim_{\rm H} G_{\Phi(a)}(K)=d+1\qquad(a\in c_0\setminus\{0\}).\]
Its range is complemented in $C(K)$ by a projection of norm at most $2$.
head: environment

label: eq:local
title: Proof
body_md:
There is $x_*\in K$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local}
\dim_{\rm H}\bigl(K\cap(x_*-r,x_*+r)\bigr)=d\qquad\text{for every }r>0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, if no such point existed, every point of $K$ would have a neighborhood whose intersection with $K$ has dimension smaller than $d$. Compactness would give a finite subcover, and finite stability would imply $\dim_{\rm H} K<d$.

Choose positive numbers $r_m<1/m$, open intervals $J_m$ with pairwise disjoint closures, and compact sets $L_m\subset K\cap J_m$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pieces}
d-\frac{d}{m+1}<d_m:=\dim_{\rm H} L_m\le d,
\qquad
\overline{J_m}\subset(x_*-r_m,x_*+r_m)\setminus\{x_*\}.
\end{equation}
To make this choice, suppose that $J_1,\ldots,J_{m-1}$ have already been chosen. Their closures are at positive distance from $x_*$, so we can choose $r_m$ as above with $(x_*-r_m,x_*+r_m)$ disjoint from all of them. By \eqref{eq:local} and $d>0$, the set
\[K\cap\bigl((x_*-r_m,x_*+r_m)\setminus\{x_*\}\bigr)\]
has dimension $d$, since removing the singleton $\{x_*\}$, of dimension zero, does not change the positive dimension $d$. Cover the punctured interval by countably many compact intervals contained in it. Countable stability supplies one of these intervals, denoted by $D_m$, for which $\dim_{\rm H}(K\cap D_m)>d-d/(m+1)$. Set $L_m=K\cap D_m$, and choose an open interval $J_m$ containing $D_m$ whose closure remains in the punctured interval. This proves \eqref{eq:pieces}. In particular, $d_m\to d$, and any sequence $z_m\in\overline{J_m}$ converges to $x_*$.

By the theorem of Bayart and Heurteaux, choose $q_m\in C(L_m)$ with $\dim_{\rm H} G_{q_m}(L_m)=d_m+1$. Since $d_m>0$, the function $q_m$ is nonzero: otherwise its graph would have dimension $d_m$. Compactness ensures that $|q_m|$ attains its positive maximum. After normalization and, if necessary, a change of sign, we may assume that $\|q_m\|_\infty=1$ and that $q_m$ takes the value $1$. Prescribe $q_m$ on $L_m$ and zero on $K\setminus J_m$. These disjoint closed subsets of $K$ carry a continuous function with values in $[-1,1]$. The bounded form of Tietze's extension theorem supplies an extension $v_m\in C(K)$ with values in $[-1,1]$. Since $v_m$ takes the value $1$ on $L_m$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vm}
v_m|_{L_m}=q_m,\qquad
\|v_m\|_\infty=1,\qquad
v_m=0\text{ on }K\setminus J_m.
\end{equation}
For $v\in C(K)$, its support is $\operatorname{supp}_K v=\overline{\{x\in K:v(x)\ne0\}}^{\,K}$, where the closure is taken in $K$. Thus the supports of the $v_m$ are contained in the pairwise disjoint sets $K\cap\overline{J_m}$.

For $j,k\in\mathbb N$, put $\ell(j,k)=2^{j-1}(2k-1)$. Every positive integer has a unique factorization as a power of $2$ times an odd positive integer. Hence the sets $\{\ell(j,k):k\in\mathbb N\}$, indexed by $j$, partition $\mathbb N$, and $\ell(j,1)\to\infty$ as $j\to\infty$. For each fixed $j$, we also have $\ell(j,k)\to\infty$ as $k\to\infty$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ej}
e_j=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{1-k}v_{\ell(j,k)}.
\end{equation}
For integers $t>r\ge0$, disjointness and \eqref{eq:vm} give
\[\left\|\sum_{k=r+1}^{t}2^{1-k}v_{\ell(j,k)}\right\|_\infty=2^{-r}.
\]
Thus the series in \eqref{eq:ej} converges uniformly, $e_j\in C(K)$, and $\|e_j\|_\infty=1$. The same disjointness gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise}
e_i(x)e_j(x)=0\quad(x\in K,\ i\ne j),
\qquad e_j(x_*)=0\quad(j\in\mathbb N).
\end{equation}

Let $a=(a_j)\in c_0$. For integers $t>r\ge0$, equations \eqref{eq:vm}--\eqref{eq:pointwise} imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:norm-finite}
\left\|\sum_{j=r+1}^{t}a_je_j\right\|_\infty
=\max_{r<j\le t}|a_j|.
\end{equation}
For the upper bound, at most one summand is nonzero at each point of $K$. For the reverse inequality, each $e_j$ takes the value $1$ at a point of $L_{\ell(j,1)}$, where all the other functions vanish. Since $a_j\to0$, the partial sums are uniformly Cauchy. We may therefore define
\[\Phi(a)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_je_j\in C(K).\]
Taking limits in \eqref{eq:norm-finite}, with $r=0$, gives $\|\Phi(a)\|_\infty=\|a\|_\infty$. Hence $\Phi$ is a linear isometry and $M:=\Phi(c_0)$ is closed.

To prove the dimension identity, let $a\ne0$ and choose $j_0$ with $a_{j_0}\ne0$. On $L_{\ell(j_0,k)}$, equations \eqref{eq:vm} and \eqref{eq:ej} give
\[\Phi(a)=a_{j_0}2^{1-k}q_{\ell(j_0,k)}.\]
For each fixed $k$, the scalar $a_{j_0}2^{1-k}$ is nonzero, so the vertical rescaling $(x,y)\mapsto(x,a_{j_0}2^{1-k}y)$ is bi-Lipschitz. Its constants may depend on $k$, which does not affect the dimension identity on each individual set. Thus
\begin{align*}
\dim_{\rm H} G_{\Phi(a)}(K)
&\ge\dim_{\rm H} G_{\Phi(a)}\bigl(L_{\ell(j_0,k)}\bigr)\\
&=\dim_{\rm H} G_{q_{\ell(j_0,k)}}\bigl(L_{\ell(j_0,k)}\bigr)
=d_{\ell(j_0,k)}+1.
\end{align*}
Since $\ell(j_0,k)\to\infty$ as $k\to\infty$, equation \eqref{eq:pieces} gives the lower bound $d+1$. The upper bound follows from \eqref{eq:upper}.

Finally, choose $t_j\in L_{\ell(j,1)}$ with $q_{\ell(j,1)}(t_j)=1$. Then $t_j\to x_*$, $e_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}$, and \eqref{eq:pointwise} gives $\Phi(a)(x_*)=0$. Define
\[B:C(K)\longrightarrow c_0,\qquad
Bf=(f(t_j)-f(x_*))_{j\ge1}.\]
Continuity of $f$ shows that $Bf\in c_0$, and
\[\|Bf\|_\infty\le2\|f\|_\infty,
\qquad B\Phi(a)=a.\]
It follows that $P_K:=\Phi B:C(K)\to M$ is bounded, $\|P_K\|\le2$, and $P_K|_M$ is the identity. Moreover, $P_K^2=\Phi B\Phi B=\Phi B=P_K$, so $P_K$ is the required projection.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $E=\{0\}$, take any compact set of Hausdorff dimension $s-1$. For $s<2$ a Cantor set of that dimension suffices, and for $s=2$ take $K=[0,1]$. There is no nonzero $h$ to check in \eqref{eq:outside}.

If $\dim E=n\ge1$, choose a basis $\{f_1,\ldots,f_n\}$ of $E$. In \cite[Proposition 3.10]{LSZ2026}, use the ambient compact set $[0,1]$ and $m=1$. Its measure hypothesis holds because $\mathcal H^{s-1}([0,1])=+\infty$ for $1<s<2$, whereas $\mathcal H^1([0,1])=1$ under our normalization. Its span hypothesis is the assumption on $E$. The resulting compact set has dimension $s-1$, and property~(3) of that proposition is \eqref{eq:outside}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $d=s-1$ and choose $K$ by \cref{lem:localization}. Apply \cref{lem:c0} to obtain $M=\Phi(c_0)\subset C(K)$. Let
\[A:C(K)\longrightarrow C[0,1]\]
be the following affine extension operator. The gaps are the connected components of the relatively open set $[0,1]\setminus K$. Each bounded interior gap is an interval $(a,b)$ with $a,b\in K$, and the possible exterior components meet $0$ or $1$ without having both endpoints in $K$. Set $Au=u$ on $K$ and
\[
(Au)(x)=\frac{b-x}{b-a}u(a)+\frac{x-a}{b-a}u(b)
\qquad(x\in(a,b))
\]
on each interior gap. On the left exterior component set $Au=u(\min K)$, and on the right exterior component set $Au=u(\max K)$.

This construction is linear and continuous on each gap and at its endpoints. To check continuity at $x\in K$, consider a sequence tending to $x$ through gaps. On any fixed gap whose closure contains $x$, the formula gives convergence to $u(x)$. Along pairwise distinct gaps, their lengths tend to zero, since they are disjoint subintervals of $[0,1]$; hence both endpoints tend to $x$. Uniform continuity of $u$ on $K$ and the convex combination in the formula again give convergence to $u(x)$. The constant exterior extensions have the same property. Thus $Au\in C[0,1]$. On every gap its values lie between the endpoint values, so $\|Au\|_\infty=\|u\|_\infty$. Consequently, $A$ is a linear isometry, and $N:=A(M)$ is closed because $M$ is complete. Set $F=E+N$.

Let $\mathcal J$ denote the family of components of $[0,1]\setminus K$. This family is countable, since each component contains a rational point and distinct components are disjoint. For $g\in N$ and $J\in\mathcal J$, write $g(x)=b_Jx+c_J$ on $J$. The affine map
\[T_J:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad
T_J(x,y)=(x,y+b_Jx+c_J)\]
has the Lipschitz inverse $T_J^{-1}(x,y)=(x,y-b_Jx-c_J)$, so it is bi-Lipschitz and maps $G_h(J)$ onto $G_{h+g}(J)$. The Lipschitz constants may depend on $J$; countable stability only requires preservation of dimension on each component separately. Therefore, for $h\in E\setminus\{0\}$, countable stability and \eqref{eq:outside} give
\begin{align*}
\dim_{\rm H} G_{h+g}([0,1]\setminus K)
&=\sup_{J\in\mathcal J}\dim_{\rm H} G_{h+g}(J)\\
&=\sup_{J\in\mathcal J}\dim_{\rm H} G_h(J)
=s.
\end{align*}
On $K$, equation \eqref{eq:upper} gives $\dim_{\rm H} G_{h+g}(K)\le d+1=s$. By finite stability, $h+g\inH_s[0,1]$.

If $h=0$ and $g\in N\setminus\{0\}$, write $g=Au$ with $u\in M\setminus\{0\}$. By \cref{lem:c0}, $\dim_{\rm H} G_g(K)=\dim_{\rm H} G_u(K)=s$. On each $J\in\mathcal J$, the graph of $g$ has dimension at most $1$. Countable stability gives $\dim_{\rm H} G_g([0,1]\setminus K)\le1$, and finite stability again gives $\dim_{\rm H} G_g([0,1])=s$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Fgood}
F\setminus\{0\}\subsetH_s[0,1].
\end{equation}

Every element of $N$ has graph dimension at most $1$ outside $K$. By \eqref{eq:outside} and $s>1$, no nonzero element of $E$ can belong to $N$. Thus $E\cap N=\{0\}$ and $F=E\oplus N$. The sum of a closed subspace and a finite-dimensional subspace is closed. The addition map $E\times N\to F$, $(h,g)\mapsto h+g$, is a bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces; by the bounded inverse theorem, this direct sum is topological. Since $N\simeq c_0$ and $E$ is finite-dimensional, we obtain
\[F\simeq E\oplus c_0\simeq c_0.\]
The last isomorphism follows by identifying $E$ with $\mathbb R^{\dim E}$ and adjoining these finitely many coordinates to a null sequence.

Let $R:C[0,1]\to C(K)$ be restriction, and let $P_K$ be the projection in \cref{lem:c0}. The operator $P_N:=AP_KR:C[0,1]\to N$ is bounded. For $g=Au\in N$, the identities $RAu=u$ and $P_Ku=u$ give $P_Ng=g$. Hence $P_N$ is a projection onto $N$.

Write $I$ for the identity operator on $C[0,1]$ and $\ker P_N=\{f\in C[0,1]:P_Nf=0\}$. The space $W:=(I-P_N)E$ is finite-dimensional and contained in $\ker P_N$. To construct a bounded projection $Q:\ker P_N\to W$, choose a basis $w_1,\ldots,w_r$ of $W$ and its coordinate functionals $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. These functionals are bounded because $W$ is finite-dimensional. By Hahn--Banach, extend them to bounded functionals $\widetilde\lambda_i$ on $\ker P_N$, and set $Qz=\sum_{i=1}^r\widetilde\lambda_i(z)w_i$. Then $Q|_W=I_W$. If $W=\{0\}$, take $Q=0$. We have $F=N\oplus W$, because each $h\in E$ decomposes as $P_Nh+(I-P_N)h$, and $N\cap W=\{0\}$. Define
\[\Pi:C[0,1]\longrightarrow F,\qquad
\Pi f=P_Nf+Q((I-P_N)f).\]
This is a bounded linear operator. For $n\in N$ and $w\in W$, it satisfies $\Pi(n+w)=n+w$. Thus it is a projection onto $F$, completing the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying \Cref{thm:main} with $E=\{0\}$ gives a closed copy of $c_0$ in $H_s[0,1]\cup\{0\}$. Since the algebraic dimension of $c_0$ is $\mathfrak c$, the existence requirement in the definition of $(\alpha,\mathfrak c)$-spaceability holds for every finite $\alpha$. The extension property follows from \Cref{thm:main}.

For the negative assertion, \cite[Theorem 2.6]{BMPS2021} supplies a dense subspace $M_0\subset C[0,1]$ of dimension $\mathfrak c$ such that $M_0\setminus\{0\}\subsetH_s[0,1]$. Indeed, that theorem imposes both Hausdorff and box dimensions equal to $s$, so its conclusion is stronger than needed here. Since $C[0,1]$ has a countable base and $M_0$ is dense, choosing one point of $M_0$ in each nonempty basic open set gives a countable dense set $\{u_j:j\in\mathbb N\}\subset M_0$. Set $D=\operatorname{span}\{u_j:j\in\mathbb N\}$. Then $D$ is dense and $\dim D=\aleph_0$: its dimension is at most countable and cannot be finite, because finite-dimensional subspaces of $C[0,1]$ are closed.

Fix $\aleph_0\le\alpha\le\mathfrak c$. Extend a Hamel basis of $D$ to one of $M_0$, and choose a subset of the latter basis of cardinality $\alpha$ containing the basis of $D$. Its span $E_\alpha$ satisfies
\[
D\subset E_\alpha\subset M_0,\qquad
\dim E_\alpha=\alpha,\qquad
E_\alpha\setminus\{0\}\subsetH_s[0,1].
\]
Any closed subspace of $C[0,1]$ containing $E_\alpha$ must contain $\overline D=C[0,1]$, and hence must equal $C[0,1]$. Such a subspace cannot have all its nonzero elements in $H_s[0,1]$, since a nonzero constant function has graph dimension $1<s$. Therefore the required closed extension fails for every infinite $\alpha$, including $\alpha=\mathfrak c$.

label: eq:polynomial-perturbation
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal P$ be the vector space of real polynomials restricted to $[0,1]$. For $p\in\mathcal P$, the map
\[
S_p:[0,1]\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow[0,1]\times\mathbb R,
\qquad S_p(x,y)=(x,y+p(x)),
\]
is bi-Lipschitz: $p$ is Lipschitz on $[0,1]$, and $S_p^{-1}=S_{-p}$ has the same property. Since $S_p$ maps $G_f([0,1])$ onto $G_{f+p}([0,1])$, invariance of Hausdorff dimension gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:polynomial-perturbation}
\dim_{\rm H} G_{f+p}([0,1])=\dim_{\rm H} G_f([0,1])
\qquad(f\in C[0,1],\ p\in\mathcal P).
\end{equation}

By \Cref{thm:main}, choose a closed subspace $F\supset E$ with $F\simeq c_0$ and $F\setminus\{0\}\subsetH_s[0,1]$. In particular, $\dim F=\mathfrak c$. Every polynomial has a graph of Hausdorff dimension $1$, because its graph parametrization $x\mapsto(x,p(x))$ is bi-Lipschitz onto its image. As $s>1$, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:polynomial-disjointness}
F\cap\mathcal P=\{0\}.
\end{equation}

The polynomials with rational coefficients form a countable dense subset of $C[0,1]$, by the Weierstrass approximation theorem and approximation of finitely many coefficients by rational numbers. Choose a sequence $(p_n)_{n\ge1}$ in which every such polynomial occurs infinitely often. Since $F$ is infinite-dimensional and $E$ is finite-dimensional, we can inductively choose
\[
h_n\in F\setminus\bigl(E+\operatorname{span}\{h_1,\ldots,h_{n-1}\}\bigr),
\qquad \|h_n\|_\infty\le\frac1n.
\]
Indeed, at each step the excluded subspace is finite-dimensional, and a nonzero vector outside it can be scaled to satisfy the norm bound.

Let $\mathcal B_E$ be a basis of $E$ (empty if $E=\{0\}$), and extend the linearly independent set $\mathcal B_E\cup\{h_n:n\ge1\}$ to a Hamel basis $\mathcal B$ of $F$. Define an algebraic linear map $T:F\to C[0,1]$ by
\[
T(h_n)=h_n+p_n\quad(n\ge1),
\qquad T(b)=b\quad\bigl(b\in\mathcal B\setminus\{h_n:n\ge1\}\bigr).
\]
Every vector has a finite expansion in $\mathcal B$, so this defines $T$ on all of $F$. No continuity of $T$ is required. We have
\[T(v)-v\in\mathcal P\qquad(v\in F).\]
If $T(v)=0$, then $v\in F\cap\mathcal P$, and \eqref{eq:polynomial-disjointness} gives $v=0$. Thus $T$ is injective. Moreover, $T$ fixes $E$, and \eqref{eq:polynomial-perturbation} shows that $T(v)\inH_s[0,1]$ whenever $v\ne0$. Hence $M:=T(F)$ satisfies
\[E\subset M,\qquad \dim M=\mathfrak c,\qquad M\setminus\{0\}\subsetH_s[0,1].\]

To verify density, fix a polynomial $p$ with rational coefficients and choose increasing indices $n_k$ with $p_{n_k}=p$. Then
\[T(h_{n_k})=h_{n_k}+p\longrightarrow p
\quad\text{uniformly on }[0,1],\]
because $\|h_{n_k}\|_\infty\le1/n_k$. Therefore $\overline M$ contains all polynomials with rational coefficients, and $\overline M=C[0,1]$.

For each $n\in\mathbb N$, applying \Cref{thm:main} to the zero subspace supplies a copy of $c_0$ whose nonzero elements belong to $H_s[0,1]$, and hence an admissible $n$-dimensional initial subspace. The dense extension just proved gives $(n,\mathfrak c)$-dense-lineability. Taking $E=\operatorname{span}\{f\}$ for each $f\inH_s[0,1]$ yields pointwise $\mathfrak c$-dense-lineability. Finally, $\dim C[0,1]=\mathfrak c$: the copy of $c_0$ gives the lower bound, while continuous functions are determined by their values on a countable dense set, giving $|C[0,1]|\le\mathfrak c$. Thus the pointwise dense-lineability is maximal.
